analysis.one_liner: Caps speculative positions in energy and farm commodity markets, including over-the-counter trades.
analysis.headline: A bill to impose limits on commodity speculation was referred to committee in July 2009 and never received a markup, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to write and enforce limits on how large a speculative position any one trader can hold in agricultural and energy commodities. Those limits would have covered not only trades on regulated exchanges but also over-the-counter deals struck privately with banks, and traders would have had to report positions so the limits could be enforced. It would also have closed a route by which foreign exchanges offering contracts tied to US prices could avoid oversight, unless they gave the CFTC the same data access as US-regulated firms. The stated goal was to curb excessive speculation, which many blamed after 2008 for sharp swings in oil and food prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that buy gasoline, heating fuel, and food, if speculation was in fact inflating prices; commercial firms like airlines, farmers, and food processors that use futures to hedge their real business risks would keep an explicit exemption and benefit from steadier markets.

how_it_helps.text: The CFTC would have had to write rules setting speculative position limits for agricultural and energy commodities no later than 90 days after enactment, and to set those limits at the minimum level practicable while leaving room for genuine hedging. [S2] [S3]

The limits would count positions across all venues — regulated exchanges, swap execution facilities, and over-the-counter derivatives — so a trader could not dodge the cap by splitting trades between public markets and private deals. [S2] [S3]

The CFTC could not grant a foreign exchange a 'no action letter' (an assurance of non-enforcement) for a contract priced off a US-regulated contract unless that exchange provided comparable data access, limiting offshoring as an escape hatch. [S2] [S3]
Positions taken as bona fide hedges of real commercial risk would be excluded from the limits, protecting businesses that buy futures to offset actual fuel or crop exposure. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large financial traders — hedge funds, index funds, and banks that deal in over-the-counter commodity derivatives — would face hard caps on how much they could bet in these markets and new reporting duties; trading firms would also bear compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large commodity speculators and swap dealers

drawbacks.text: The bill required position limits set at the 'minimum level practicable' while preserving liquidity for hedging; in a market the size of oil or grains, overly tight limits could reduce liquidity and widen bid-ask spreads, raising hedging costs for the very commercial firms the bill meant to protect. [S3]

The bill's definition of a bona fide hedge excluded trades made to offset financial risk from an over-the-counter commodity derivative, so some commercial users managing risk through private deals would have had those positions counted against them. [S3]

Economists disagreed sharply at the time over how much speculation actually drives commodity prices; if speculation was not the main cause of price swings, the caps would have added compliance burden without delivering much price relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill took a direct, structural approach: hard position limits across every trading venue, with reporting to enforce them and an exemption for genuine hedgers. The main risks were design ones — limits could thin out market liquidity, and some commercial firms' hedges through private deals would not be exempt. It never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee in July 2009, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Susan Collins introduced the bill on July 8, 2009. [S1] [S5]
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. [S5]
No cosponsors ever joined the bill. [S4]
The action history shows no further steps — no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large commodity speculators and banks dealing in over-the-counter derivatives kept operating without position limits in US agricultural and energy markets for the rest of that Congress; nobody paid the compliance costs, but consumers got no protections from this bill either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big commodity speculators and swap dealers

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap speculative positions in agricultural and energy commodities and referred it to committee.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill — no markup, no vote, no report — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes occurred. A Republican introduced the bill but attracted zero cosponsors of either party, so the fight never took a partisan shape.

industries.industry: Hedge funds, index traders, and other large commodity speculators
industries.note: Hard caps on net long or net short positions in farm and energy commodities, counting every venue together, would directly limit the size of their bets. Their unrestricted position was the thing the bill existed to restrain.

industries.industry: Banks and dealers in over-the-counter commodity derivatives
industries.note: Private commodity derivatives would have been folded into position limits and reporting for the first time, closing the off-exchange escape from regulation. Their profits from trading these products depended on staying outside exchange limits.
The bill would deny them no-action letters unless they handed the CFTC data access comparable to US firms', raising the cost of marketing contracts that let speculators sidestep US rules.

industries.industry: Commercial hedgers (airlines, farmers, food processors, fuel buyers)
industries.note: Genuine hedges of real business risk would be explicitly exempt from the caps, and if speculation was inflating prices, steadier markets would lower their input costs and consumers' prices.
